Integrate

IN-tih-grayt — starts like 'integer,' a whole number; to integrate is to make things whole together. · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To integrate to combine separate parts so that they work together as one whole.

The two departments worked all year to integrate their separate computer systems into one.

Worked Example

A new student moves to a school partway through the year, knowing no one. By spring, she has joined the debate team, eats lunch with a steady group of friends, and volunteers with the yearbook club.

She has become a working part of the school community — she has integrated into it. Unlike 'attend,' which just means showing up, to integrate means becoming a joined, functioning part of the whole.

How Integrate Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

combine

combine: to join separate things together

incorporate

incorporate: to include as part of a whole

unify

unify: to make into a single unit

Antonyms

separate

separate: to keep or set apart

segregate

segregate: to set apart from the main group

How Strong Is It? — add → integrate → merge

add vs. integrate

add vs. integrate: To add something is weaker than to integrate it — adding just places it alongside the rest, while integrating actually makes it a working part of the whole.

merge vs. integrate

merge vs. integrate: To merge is stronger than to integrate: integrating joins parts so they function together, but merging can blend them so completely that the original separate parts disappear.

Build the Word

The pieces

root — integr-

root — integr-: whole, complete (Latin)

suffix — -ate

suffix — -ate: to make or do (Latin)

Put it together

Put it together: Latin integer meant 'whole, untouched.' To integrate something is to make it part of a whole rather than leaving it separate.
